scenes.title: Keep the learning service available
scenes.visual_direction: Availability begins with a user completing a useful task.
scenes.narration_en_US: Welcome to Northstar Learning Center. Tally is helping the school protect a simple promise: students can reach the services they need. Learning access means opening a lesson and continuing useful work. Enrollment means choosing a class and receiving a reliable confirmation. Availability describes whether an authorized user can obtain that service when needed. A server can have power, answer a basic check, and still fail this promise if students cannot finish enrollment. Our lesson is about denial of service and distributed denial of service. We will connect each mechanism to a limited resource, examine evidence, and choose a control that can reach that resource. Every campus incident in this lesson is simulated output. The files support offline reasoning; they are not reports of a real school attack. By the end, you should explain what is constrained, which observations support that conclusion, and how to check recovery. Begin with the student's task. The most impressive traffic chart matters only when we can explain its relationship to the service people actually need.

scenes.title: Trace the complete service path
scenes.visual_direction: A service depends on a chain of reachable resources.
scenes.narration_en_US: Follow one student opening the Northstar portal. Name lookup translates the portal name into an address the client can use. The network path carries packets between the student and the service. A connection lets the endpoints organize their exchange. The application checks the request, obtains needed data, and returns a useful result. These steps can depend on other services, including identity and storage. A failure anywhere along this path can prevent enrollment. That is why a healthy application processor does not prove that the whole service is reachable. Likewise, a busy network link does not tell us whether the application itself has a defect. Tally draws each dependency as a separate box so we can ask a precise question at every boundary: what entered, what completed, and what waited or failed? This map is a starting model, not a complete inventory of every real deployment. During an actual authorized assessment, confirm the architecture with its owner. Here, we use the supplied fictional map and keep every investigation inside the offline evidence package.

scenes.title: Measure the user's result
scenes.visual_direction: Compare user outcomes inside an explicitly defined observation window.
scenes.narration_en_US: Before diagnosing a traffic pattern, define the result we want to protect. Success means a specified task reached its intended endpoint. For enrollment, that could mean receiving a confirmation, rather than merely loading the first page. Delay describes how long the task takes. Record the part being timed and whether failed attempts are included. Errors describe failed outcomes, with enough detail to distinguish a rejected connection from an application response. The time window places these observations on a shared clock. A one minute traffic average cannot be compared casually with a whole day of help desk tickets. Our fixtures provide aligned sixty second windows where stated. We will also keep the number of attempted user checks visible so a success fraction has a clear denominator. These are simulated observations, not a promise about production performance. A good incident note can therefore say which task failed, for how many sampled attempts, during which interval. That statement gives the resource measurements a purpose and lets another analyst check the reasoning without guessing what the chart represents.

scenes.title: Keep the assessment inside its authority
scenes.visual_direction: This lesson analyzes local fixtures without generating network traffic.
scenes.narration_en_US: Availability testing can affect other people's work, so authority must describe the action, not just the topic. Written scope identifies the owner, systems, permitted methods, time, and responsible contacts. In this course package, our authorized action is reading and analyzing offline evidence. We do not send packets, replay captures, contact reflectors, or load a public service. Stop conditions belong in any future separately approved exercise: unexpected impact, loss of monitoring, or uncertainty about the target should trigger the agreed response. Evidence custody means keeping the original fixture, its label, and the analysis result distinguishable. A generated table remains simulated output even when a parser successfully reads it. A proposed control remains a proposal until it is tested under its own authority. These distinctions protect both people and the quality of our conclusions. Tally keeps the scope card beside the technical diagram because a familiar tool does not grant permission. You can complete every learner task in this film using local files and written reasoning. No live disruption is needed to understand the mechanisms.

scenes.title: Ask four questions from first principles
scenes.visual_direction: Select protection by explaining the constrained resource first.
scenes.narration_en_US: Our working method has four questions. Resource asks what finite thing the service needs: link capacity, packet processing, connection memory, or application work. Demand asks how much of that resource arriving work requires, and for how long. Evidence asks what we observed at a named location, with units and a time window. Control asks which change can reduce the relevant demand, preserve useful work, or increase appropriate capacity. Work through these questions in order. Buying a faster server may leave an upstream link full. Dropping packets on a server may save application work while leaving that same access link congested. A control can be useful without protecting every resource in the path. We will use four connected Northstar cases to practice choosing the right boundary. Their observations are simulated output, and their proposed improvements require separate validation. The method also leaves room for uncertainty: when a record cannot establish intent or causation, say so. A well bounded conclusion is more useful than a confident attack label that the available measurements cannot support.

scenes.title: Separate the outcome from the cause
scenes.visual_direction: An availability symptom supports investigation before attribution.
scenes.narration_en_US: Service failure is an observed outcome: a legitimate user cannot obtain the expected service. Resource pressure is one possible explanation, such as a full link or an exhausted connection queue. A mechanism explains how particular work consumes that resource. Intent asks whether someone deliberately caused the harmful condition. These are related questions, but they need different evidence. A popular class opening can create heavy demand. A software problem can waste capacity. A hostile flood can also overwhelm a service. Similar charts may appear in each situation. When we use the term denial of service attack, we are describing deliberate interference with availability; a slow page alone does not establish that conclusion. Start the Northstar record with the task and symptom, then test resource explanations. Keep suspicious behavior as a hypothesis until the evidence supports it. This approach does not require waiting to protect users. An owner may apply an appropriate protective control while attribution remains open. Document the operational reason for that action and keep the later conclusion tied to the facts actually available.

scenes.title: Read rates with their units
scenes.visual_direction: Different rate units describe different kinds of work.
scenes.narration_en_US: Bits per second measures a volume of transmitted data over time. Packets per second counts packets over time. Requests per second counts application requests over time. Each can be important, and none is a universal substitute for the others. Many small packets can require substantial packet processing without consuming the same byte volume as large packets. One application request can require much more work than another. A connection can contain several requests, and network retransmissions can add packets without adding new user tasks. Before comparing measurements, choose the same window and confirm the observation point. Also name the counted layer. Internet protocol bytes and Ethernet bytes include different information, so a calculation must keep that definition consistent. In Northstar case one, the stated rates use Internet protocol octets converted to bits per second across aligned sixty second windows. That definition makes its arithmetic checkable. When a dashboard uses a different basis, record it rather than silently combining unlike counters. Units are part of the evidence, not decoration beside a number.

scenes.title: Understand finite capacity and waiting work
scenes.visual_direction: Persistent excess demand grows waiting work or forces rejection.
scenes.narration_en_US: Imagine a service desk that can finish a limited amount of work each second. Arrival brings new work to that desk. Capacity describes what the resource can handle under the stated conditions. A queue holds work that cannot be handled immediately. Completion removes finished work. If arrivals keep requiring more work than the desk can supply, the queue cannot grow forever. A bounded system eventually delays, rejects, or drops some work. This picture explains a mechanism; it is not a measured performance model for every computer. Real services have several queues, shared resources, and variable request costs. Even a short burst can fill a small queue while a long average looks comfortable. For Northstar, we therefore ask both how much work arrived and what happened to waiting work. We also check whether useful completions continued. A capacity number without its conditions is incomplete. A queue count without its limit is difficult to interpret. Keeping arrival, capacity, waiting, and completion separate helps us locate the constraint before choosing an intervention.

scenes.title: Describe distribution without inventing identity
scenes.visual_direction: Traffic distribution and actor identity are different conclusions.
scenes.narration_en_US: A denial of service attack may originate from one source. A distributed denial of service attack coordinates activity across many sources. Distribution can make simple source blocking less effective, but the resource being exhausted still needs to be identified. An observed address is a value recorded at a particular point in the network. It is not automatically a person, a device count, or proof of control. Address sharing can place many clients behind one address. A single device may use several addresses, and some packet sources can be forged. Attribution connects the harmful activity to an actor and requires evidence beyond a source list. In this lesson, a drawing with many devices explains a possible distributed architecture. It does not establish that the Northstar fixture came from a botnet. We will keep that distinction visible in every case. First describe the traffic pattern that is supported. Then state what additional evidence would be needed for a stronger conclusion. Operational protection can focus on harmful resource consumption while the identity and coordination questions remain unresolved.

scenes.title: Build a map of resource exhaustion
scenes.visual_direction: The same availability failure can begin at different resource limits.
scenes.narration_en_US: Use four resource families to organize the next chapters. Bandwidth limits the data that a link can carry. Packet work limits how quickly a device can inspect and forward arriving packets. Connection state uses memory and bookkeeping for communication that is pending or established. Application work includes the processing and dependencies needed to answer a request. These families can interact. A single incident may stress several of them, and a control may move the bottleneck to another place. The map is therefore an analysis aid, not a rule that every event belongs to exactly one box. For example, packets bearing a synchronize flag might fill a server's pending connection state, or their arrival rate might overwhelm an intermediate device first. The packet name does not decide which mechanism dominates. Tally will keep the resource map available as we inspect each Northstar fixture. Choose a hypothesis by correlating measurements at the relevant boundary. The next step is to examine network capacity, then compare that pattern with connection state pressure on a link that still has room.

scenes.title: Read Northstar's constrained access link
scenes.visual_direction: An ingress cap can hide a much larger offered load upstream.
scenes.narration_en_US: Northstar case one begins with three aligned sixty second windows. All of these values are simulated output. Baseline traffic offers fifty megabits per second to a campus access link with a capacity of two hundred megabits per second. Normal enrollment offers one hundred fifty megabits per second. Increased demand during enrollment fits inside this stated link budget. In the incident window, the provider observes offered load of two thousand four hundred megabits per second toward the campus. Accepted load at the constrained ingress is two hundred megabits per second. These figures describe different observation points. The campus value does not mean that only two hundred megabits per second tried to arrive. In this fixture, the difference is an equivalent discarded rate of two thousand two hundred megabits per second at the constrained ingress. Keep the labels attached to the numbers as Tally draws the link. The evidence supports severe capacity pressure at this boundary. It does not identify an attacker, explain every discarded packet, or establish the exact experience of every student.

scenes.title: Connect the link evidence to user impact
scenes.visual_direction: A lightly loaded server can sit behind an unavailable access path.
scenes.narration_en_US: The provider view and the campus view answer different questions. The provider view describes traffic offered toward the access boundary. The ingress limit describes the maximum rate accepted through that constrained point in our fixture. Discarded traffic is the equivalent rate that does not pass this boundary during the same window. The server view describes a downstream machine after this loss has already occurred. In Northstar case one, server processor use is twenty five percent, while only twenty of one hundred simulated user checks succeed. Those facts can coexist: a server cannot process requests that fail to reach it. Low processor use therefore does not clear the network path. At the same time, the success fraction is a sampled outcome, not proof that every failure has one cause. Preserve its denominator and time window. The analysis should connect the provider record, campus counters, and client checks, while retaining their separate meanings. This is how a resource explanation becomes useful: it accounts for both the constrained link and the otherwise puzzling downstream observation without inventing actor identity.

scenes.title: Count packet handling as well as bytes
scenes.visual_direction: A device may reach its packet-processing limit before its bit-rate limit.
scenes.narration_en_US: Packet size affects how many packets carry a given amount of data. Packet rate tells us how many individual packets arrive each second. Processing cost includes the work a device performs for those packets, such as examining headers or checking a rule. A measured limit tells us what that specific device and configuration can sustain under defined conditions. Consequently, a link that looks comfortable in bits per second can still carry more packets than a component can handle. This is a general resource model, not a measured finding about the Northstar router. Packet sizes, hardware paths, enabled features, and traffic mix all affect real performance. We would need relevant device counters and an authorized measurement before asserting its actual limit. Do not borrow a marketing throughput number and treat it as the answer for every packet pattern. In an incident record, place byte rate beside packet rate, drops, and device health. That combination helps distinguish a full transmission link from overloaded packet processing. It also explains why two traffic streams with similar byte volume may have different effects.

scenes.title: Understand direct and coordinated traffic
scenes.visual_direction: Multiple senders can combine pressure at one constrained destination path.
scenes.narration_en_US: Direct traffic reaches a destination without first using another service to reflect replies toward it. That describes a traffic path, not permission or intent. The defender may then face combined demand larger than any one device contributes. This diagram explains the architecture without teaching how to build or operate it. Source uncertainty still matters. A set of addresses in a flow record does not prove that each address represents a compromised device or that one actor coordinates them. For Northstar case one, the supplied evidence establishes offered and accepted rates, sampled user impact, and downstream processor use. It does not supply device compromise records or a command channel investigation. Keep the traffic hypothesis and the attribution question separate. Protecting the constrained access path can be justified by the availability evidence itself. Later chapters will examine how reflected traffic changes the path and why defense responsibilities can sit with several different network operators.

scenes.title: Place protection before the constrained resource
scenes.visual_direction: A control must act early enough to spare the resource at risk.
scenes.narration_en_US: Suppose Northstar applies a campus filter after its constrained access boundary. That filter may protect a downstream application or reduce later processing. It cannot undo the capacity already consumed while unwanted traffic approached and crossed the protected link. An upstream filter can act before that access constraint, provided the upstream operator can distinguish the traffic appropriately and has the capacity to handle it. This placement principle explains why an owner may need provider coordination during a volumetric event. It does not promise that a particular filter will preserve every legitimate request. Rules need evidence, an accountable owner, and a way to check unintended impact. The user outcome remains the deciding measure: can students complete the intended task after protection is applied? For Northstar, any recovery rows in the supplied package are simulated output, not a report of an installed filter. We will discuss control selection and escalation more fully later. For now, keep one causal question beside the diagram: does this control reduce demand before the resource we are trying to protect is consumed?

scenes.title: Follow a normal TCP handshake

Acknowledge marks the client's confirming reply. The server can then regard the connection as established. Pending state represents the server's temporary bookkeeping while it awaits that confirmation. It does not authenticate the human using the connection. A completed handshake also does not prove that a later application request is harmless. For availability analysis, notice the timing of resource commitment. Depending on the implementation and active defenses, a server may reserve resources before the final confirmation arrives. That gap creates the connection state question we will examine next. Tally keeps the pending box separate from the established box so completed connections and incomplete attempts are never silently counted as the same thing.

scenes.narration_en_US: Question 3. The provider observes twenty-four hundred megabits per second offered to Northstar's two-hundred-megabit connection. The campus accepts two hundred, and user checks fail. Which action best addresses that constrained connection? A. A web filter after the link can protect application work but cannot recover bandwidth already consumed on that link. Spare processor capacity does not establish that users can reach the service. The proposed provider action still needs authorization, a suitable traffic-selection method, and checks for legitimate-user impact. The fixture distinguishes offered traffic at the provider from accepted traffic at campus in the same interval. It supports the location of the bottleneck in this simulated case, without proving an attacker's identity or the effectiveness of an untested control.

In live telemetry, check counter definitions and interval boundaries before applying the same division. Attempts that cross an interval boundary or repeated records can otherwise change its meaning. Our result describes the constructed window rather than an observed live server.
